https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/22/orba.text: Menü Kereső Éjszakánként 1,5 millió forintba került Orbán Viktor szállása Svájcban, Havasi szerint ott ilyenek az árak Belföld Cseke Balázs Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kimagasló áron szállt meg Orbán Viktor Svájcban a januári davosi Világgazdasági Fórum idején. A volt miniszterelnök kilencfős delegációjának elszállásolása közel 20 millió forintba került három éjszakára, Orbán lakosztálya éjszakánként 1,5 millió forint volt, derült ki abból a közadatigénylésből, amit Hadházy Ákos korábbi országgyűlési képviselő nyújtott be. Havasi Bertalan, a Fidesz kommunikációs igazgatója az RTL Híradónak úgy reagált, hogy minden delegáció ennyi pénzért tudott megszállni, mert „Svájcban a davosi fórum idején ilyenek az árak”. Csakhogy ez nem igaz, a csatorna gyűjtése szerint más delegációk ennél jóval olcsóbban is foglalt szállodai szobát. Argentinában botrány lett abból, hogy az elnök éjszakánként 620 ezer forintért szállt meg a svájci fórum idején, Dánia 132,8 ezer forintért foglalt szobát, de az utolsó pillanatban lemondták az utat, mert ezt is túl drágának találták. Bermuda miniszterelnöke éjszakánként 62 ezer forintot fizetett, a michigani kormányzó szállása pedig 59,1 ezer forintba került. Ehhez képest Orbán Viktor szobája a zürichi The Dolder Grand Hotelben éjszakánként 1,5 millió forint volt. Hadházy Ákos januárban fordult a Külgazdasági és Külügyminisztériumhoz, hogy kiderüljön, mennyi közpénzbe került Orbánék svájci szállása, de nem kapott választ. A független képviselő ezért pert indított, ami már a kormányváltás után zárult le: végül a tárca jogutódja, a Külügyminisztérium adta ki a kért adatokat. A számla végösszege bruttó 48 530 svájci frankra, azaz januári árfolyammal számolva több mint 20 millió forintra rúgott. A tételek között szerepelt a hotel saját, két Michelin-csillagos éttermében elfogyasztott étkezések ára is, ez összesen majdnem 1,8 millió forintba került. A tételes elszámolásban látszik, hogy a szobákba is rendeltek italokat és rágcsálnivalókat, összesen nagyjából 89 ezer forint értékben, és a mosodai szolgáltatást is igénybe vették, 125 ezer forintért. Hadházy Ákos az RTL-nek arról beszélt: egy ország miniszterelnöke egy normális szobában is tudna aludni, és semmi szükség nem lenne 1-200 négyzetméteres lakosztályra komornyikkal. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmde.text: By Joshua Cheetham ,Â Thomas Copeland Â and Â Alison Benjamin ,Â BBC Verify Published 16 October 2026, 06:00 BST The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows. Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks. Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks. As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests. BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported. Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes. Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts. The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners". Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby. The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard. Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said. Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route". Oil shipments stall Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen. About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day. The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August. Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman. These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore. So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships. Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day". "The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added. The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media. Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman. A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard. Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said. Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship. https://praguemonitor.com/work-life/apos.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points An apostille is a single certificate, issued by the country where a public document was made, that lets another Hague Convention state accept it without further consular legalisation. Countries outside the Convention require full legalisation through their foreign ministry and a Czech embassy; some EU and treaty arrangements remove the formality for certain documents. The usual order is: obtain the original, authenticate it in the issuing country, then have it translated into Czech by a sworn translator. On this page 7 sections Two systems, one purpose When Czechia asks for it EU and treaty shortcuts The sequence that works Where it goes wrong Do it yourself or use an agent Documents that go the other way A Czech office has no way to know whether a stamp on a certificate from a distant country is genuine. It cannot call the registrar in another country, and it cannot recognise a signature from a town it has never heard of. Authentication is the system that closes that gap: someone competent in the issuing country vouches for the official who signed, so that the Czech clerk does not have to. Which documents require authentication and what form it takes depends on the office and the procedure; confirm with the Ministry of the Interior or the authority that asked for the paper. Two systems, one purpose There are two methods of authenticating a public document for use abroad. Both prove that the signature, the capacity of the signatory and the seal on the document are genuine. Neither proves that the content is true. Apostille. Under the Hague Convention of 1961 abolishing the requirement of legalisation for foreign public documents, countries that belong to the Convention issue an apostille: a standard certificate, attached to the document, from a competent authority in the country that made it. A document with an apostille is accepted in any other Convention state without further steps. Czechia is a party, and so are most countries that Czech residents come from, including the United Kingdom, the United States, Ukraine, India and most of Europe. For US papers such as the FBI record, see our guide for Americans in Czechia . The Hague Conference's website lists the states that are parties and the authorities that issue apostilles in each. Legalisation. If the country that issued the document is not part of the Convention, the document goes through a chain: certification by an authority in the issuing country, typically the foreign ministry, and then legalisation by the Czech embassy or consulate that covers that country. This is slower and costs more. Some countries and some documents have bilateral arrangements that replace the chain with something simpler, and the Czech embassy can say which applies. Apostille, legalisation and exemption Feature Apostille Full legalisation Exempt When Issuing country is in the Hague Convention Issuing country is outside the Convention A treaty or EU rule removes the formality Who authenticates A designated authority in the issuing country The issuing country's foreign ministry, then the Czech embassy No one Steps One Two or more None Typical delay Days to weeks Weeks None A summary. Procedures and delays vary by country; check the issuing authority and the Czech embassy. When Czechia asks for it Authentication is needed when a foreign public document is submitted to a Czech office as proof of a fact. The common cases for newcomers are residence applications, including family reunification (marriage and birth certificates, criminal-record extracts), applications for permanent residence and citizenship, recognition of qualifications, registering a marriage or a birth with Czech authorities, and some company and property transactions. The office's checklist says which papers need it. If the checklist is silent, ask. Public documents are the ones issued by an authority or a notary: civil-status certificates, court judgments, police and criminal-record extracts, diplomas issued by a state institution, notarised copies and powers of attorney. A private document, such as a letter from a friend or an employer's reference, is not apostilled in the same way, although a notary can certify a signature on it, and the notary's act can then be authenticated. Documents also have a lifespan. For residence applications, supporting documents are generally accepted only if no older than 180 days when filed, with exceptions such as passports and civil-status certificates, and a certificate that states a shorter validity of its own is held to that (as of 2026; check MV). The authenticated version has to arrive in time, so read the limit before you order. EU and treaty shortcuts Within the EU, Regulation (EU) 2016/1191, in application since 16 February 2019, removes the apostille and legalisation requirement for certain public documents issued in one member state and used in another, such as birth, death, marriage and registered-partnership certificates and criminal-record extracts. It also allows multilingual standard forms to cut translation needs. If your document comes from an EU country, ask the Czech office whether it accepts it under the Regulation. Several bilateral treaties on legal assistance between Czechia and other countries also waive legalisation for some documents; the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs publish lists. Do not assume an exemption. If the office wants an apostille and you do not have one, the file waits. Ask first, and keep the reply in writing. The sequence that works From foreign original to Czech file Get the right original Order a recent, official copy from the issuing authority. A photocopy or a printout of a scan does not qualify. Find the competent authority In an apostille country, check which office issues apostilles for that type of document (often a foreign ministry, a court or a state office). Authenticate Obtain the apostille, or follow the legalisation chain through the foreign ministry and the Czech embassy. Translate Give the authenticated document, with the apostille, to a sworn translator for a Czech translation. Check the date and the set Make sure the document is within its age limit and the translation is bound to the original. The order is not arbitrary. The apostille attaches to the original, and the sworn translator must see the finished document, including the apostille, because the apostille itself is translated. Translating before authenticating wastes the translation. Read our explainer on sworn translations for the second half. A hypothetical example: a software engineer from outside Europe needs a marriage certificate and a criminal-record extract for a family permit application. She orders both in week one, authenticates each in weeks two to five, because the extract has to go through a separate agency, then takes both to a sworn translator in week six, and files in week eight. The marriage certificate would have kept; the extract has a maximum age, so she timed its ordering to leave a margin. Where it goes wrong The mistakes are repetitive. The apostille is attached to a photocopy, not the original or a certified copy. The apostille is issued by the wrong authority. The document is authenticated, then it is found to be too old. The translation is dated before the apostille and so does not cover it. The name on the certificate differs from the passport and no explanation is attached. And the applicant relies on an agency that charges for steps that a ministry would do for little, or promises results no one can promise. If an office rejects a document, ask for the reason in writing. Sometimes the answer is that a second apostille is required for a copy, or that the authority wants the original returned with a new translation. These are fixable, but fixing them after the deadline is expensive. The guides to bringing a spouse and to permanent residence show how often the same step recurs, and getting a criminal-record certificate covers the most time-sensitive one. Authenticate the original, not the copy An apostille certifies the signature and seal on the document it is attached to. If you authenticate a copy that the Czech office will not accept, the apostille goes with it. Check whether the office wants an original, a certified copy or a notarised copy before you start. Do it yourself or use an agent Most apostilles can be obtained directly from the issuing authority, often by post or online, at a modest official fee. Agents exist who will collect, authenticate and translate documents for you, and they can save real time if you are abroad, short of time or dealing with several countries. Judge them as you would any intermediary: ask who actually performs each step, what the total price is, what happens if the Czech office rejects the result, and whether they work with a court translator ( soudní překladatel ) on the Ministry of Justice register. An agent cannot make a document older than the age limit or turn a copy into an original. Documents that go the other way The same logic applies in reverse. A Czech document that you need abroad, such as a Czech birth certificate or a criminal-record extract from the Czech register, is authenticated by Czech authorities. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs issues apostilles for most Czech public documents, and the Ministry of Justice for court and notarial documents (as of 2026; check which one covers your paper). If you plan to use a Czech paper in another country, ask the authority there which version it needs and whether it needs a translation. Frequently asked questions What is an apostille? A standard certificate issued by a competent authority in the country that made a public document, which lets other Hague Convention states accept it without further legalisation. Is Czechia part of the Apostille Convention? Yes. Documents from other Convention states with an apostille are accepted, subject to the receiving office's rules. Do I translate before or after the apostille? After. The sworn translator needs the authenticated document so that the apostille is translated too. Do EU documents need an apostille? Often not. EU Regulation 2016/1191 removes the formality for certain civil-status documents and extracts between member states. Ask the Czech office. This is a general explainer, not legal or tax advice.
